o: Each operation deletes a duplicate occurrence of some character next to another occurrence of the same character. No operation can ever remove the *last* copy of a character, because an operation always needs another occurrence of `c` adjacent to anchor on. Conversely, if a character appears multiple times, we can always shrink duplicates away one by one. So the answer is simply the number of **distinct** characters in `s`. In "aaabc" the distinct characters are a, b, c → 3; in "cbbd" they are c, b, d → 3; in "baadccab" they are b, a, d, c → 4, matching all examples. With `|s| ≤ 100` even simulation works, but the distinct-count observation gives an O(n) solution.
k: An operation can never delete the final occurrence of a character, so every character keeps at least one copy.

a.i: Since every character must retain exactly one surviving copy and duplicates are always removable, the minimized length equals the size of the character set of `s`. We can compute this with a hash set or a fixed-size boolean array over the 26 lowercase letters.
s: Insert every character of s into a set (or mark a boolean[26] array).
Return the size of the set.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the string

a.i: Faithfully apply the operations: repeatedly, whenever a character occurs more than once, remove one duplicate occurrence (any neighbor-based deletion reduces to this). The process terminates when all remaining characters are distinct.
s: While some character appears more than once, delete one extra occurrence.

w: The key interview insight is proving the lower bound (last copies survive) matches the upper bound (duplicates die). Edge cases: single-character strings return 1; strings of all identical characters return 1. Follow-up: what if operations could delete without needing a neighbor occurrence? Then the answer could drop further, so the adjacency rule is essential.
